title: The record spans six continents, not five
published: Since 1983, more than 70 employment audit experiments, carried out in more than 26 countries across [[five]] continents, have randomized the gender of fictitious applicants to measure the extent of hiring discrimination on the basis of gender.
corrected: Since 1983, more than 70 employment audit experiments, carried out in more than 26 countries across [[six]] continents, have randomized the gender of fictitious applicants to measure the extent of hiring discrimination on the basis of gender.
note: The paper's own evidence map, fig. S2.2, is drawn as six continent facets: Africa, Asia, Europe, N. America, Oceania, S. America. Section S2 names Oceania among the regions where the boom in audit experimentation occurred, and the earliest study in the whole record, the Australian one the introduction discusses, is on that continent. The sentence describes the wider literature rather than the 57 studies reanalysed here, but a superset of those studies cannot span fewer continents, so five is too few under any reading.

title: Table S2.1 overstates the occupation counts for two studies
published:
Gonzalez et al. (89): Spain ... [[18]] occupations

Dahl and Krog (84): Denmark ... [[24]] occupations
corrected:
Gonzalez et al. (89): Spain ... [[17]] occupations

Dahl and Krog (84): Denmark ... [[21]] occupations
note: The article disagrees with itself in these two rows. Figs. S4.37 and S4.32 plot 17 and 21 occupations for the same two studies, and 17 and 21 is what the deposited data hold. The other 55 rows of the column are right. The table is not reprinted here because its N subjects column cannot be regenerated from the deposit, which carries no subject counts.

title: Table 2's Model 2 intercept carries no significance marker
published: Table 2, Model 2, intercept: −3.72 (1.13), [[carrying no significance marker]]
corrected: Table 2, Model 2, intercept: −3.72 (1.13), [[carrying the two-asterisk marker the table's own note gives for P < 0.01]]
note: The Model 2 intercept is printed as −3.72 with no marker, at a p-value of 0.00104. Five decimals rather than the three the table's own note uses: at three the p-value reads 0.001, which is the threshold for the third star rather than the second, and the correction would be ambiguous inside the rule it is being compared against. The numerically identical Model 3 intercept, −3.73, does carry its two stars. The estimate and its standard error are right and only the marker is missing, so what is corrected here is the table rather than any sentence.

corrected: The PRISMA search process yielded over 70 papers that met our inclusion criteria. Figure S6.[[63]] is a "PRISMA flow diagram" that illustrates the search strategy and reports the number of records retained at each stage of the process.
note: The supplementary materials list Figs. S1.1 to S6.63 in their front matter, and the PRISMA flow diagram is the last of them. There is no fig. S6.66. The same paragraph cites the evidence map as fig. S.2.2, where the figure itself is numbered S2.2.

published: The magnitude of these biases is higher in women-dominated occupations than in men-dominated occupations, by a statistically significant [[2.10]] points (bootstrapped SE: 0.58), perhaps suggesting that pro--status quo forces operate differently across contexts.
corrected: The magnitude of these biases is higher in women-dominated occupations than in men-dominated occupations, by a statistically significant [[2.11]] points (bootstrapped SE: 0.58), perhaps suggesting that pro--status quo forces operate differently across contexts.
note: The deposited code and the maintained rewrite both give 2.10547, which rounds to 2.11 at the two decimal places the sentence prints. The published figure is the truncation rather than a different number, and the bootstrapped standard error, 0.5781, is 0.58 as published.

title: Figure 4 colors imputed gender composition categories as though the study authors had given them
published: The gender composition categories ([[as given by study authors where available and by us otherwise]]) are distinguished by color and shape (green circles, men-dominated; orange triangles, gender-balanced; blue squares, [[women-dominated]]).
corrected: The gender composition categories ([[as given by study authors]]) are distinguished by color and shape (green circles, men-dominated; orange triangles, gender-balanced; blue squares, [[women-dominated; grey circles, category not given by the study authors]]).
note: Of the 298 study-occupation cells the figure draws, only 174 carry a gender composition category the original study's own authors assigned; the remaining 124 were filled in by us from where the occupation falls in the ILO gender distribution. The caption discloses that in words, so the article is accurate about what it did, but the figure gives all 298 points the same three colors, and a color is a claim about the occupation that a reader cannot tell apart from the 174 that were coded. The corrected figure draws the 124 imputed cells in grey, keeping their position, their interval and their weight. NO ESTIMATE MOVES: the meta-regression is fitted on the continuous share of women in the occupation and never on the category, so Tables 1 and 2, the gender gradient and every study-level effect in the supplementary materials are exactly as published. What changes is which of 298 points is which color. The coding is the same authors' own, carried back from the successor project, where the distinction is kept as a column and the imputed categories are dropped rather than plotted.

title: Figure S1.1 prints a clipped estimate for Neumark et al.
published: Fig. S1.1, Neumark et al. (9): United States: [[2.3]] (8.4)
corrected: Fig. S1.1, Neumark et al. (9): United States: [[−12.3]] (8.4)
note: The figure's own text carries the right number and the page does not print it. Read off the glyphs, the row holds exactly 2 . 3 space ( 8 . 4 ) beginning at x0 = 268.50, which is where every other three-character value in the column begins, and no minus and no 1 is inked anywhere to its left: the short dash that sits there is the row's axis tick, which the positive rows carry too. The authors' own field_ates_plot.pdf is the same in both respects, so the leading −1 was lost when the figure was drawn rather than when it was composed: the label overflows the plot panel and its −1 is clipped out of the ink, while the text layer keeps it, which is why pdftotext reports −12.3 for a page that shows 2.3 and why a token gate cannot see this defect at all. Nothing about the estimate is in doubt. The article's own introduction prints it as (−12.3 points, SE: 8.4 points) and the deposit gives −12.307692 (8.384118), so the paper disagrees with itself the way entry 2 records for table S2.1. The corrected figure is the maintained pipeline's own, which draws the full value: of the 420 words and numbers it carries, 419 are on the published page and the one exception is the restored −12.3.

title: Reference 9 separates two coauthors with a semicolon
published: 9. D. [[Neumark;]] R. J. Bank, K. D. Van Nort, Sex discrimination in restaurant hiring: An audit study. Q. J. Econ. 111, 915–941 (1996).
corrected: 9. D. Neumark, R. J. Bank, K. D. Van Nort, Sex discrimination in restaurant hiring: An audit study. Q. J. Econ. 111, 915–941 (1996).
note: The entry names three coauthors and separates the first two with a semicolon and the second two with a comma, so it is inconsistent with itself before it is compared with anything. Crossref, doi 10.2307/2946676: David Neumark, Roy J. Bank and Kyle D. Van Nort are three authors of one article, Q. J. Econ. 111, 915-941 (1996). Every one of the other 127 entries in this list separates its authors with commas, and the supplementary materials set this same reference with a comma. The defect is specific to the article's printing of it.

title: Reference 71 in the supplementary materials drops the period after its number
published: [[71]] S. Baert, A.-S. De Pauw, N. Deschacht, Do employer preferences contribute to sticky floors? ILR Rev. 69, 714–736 (2016).
corrected: 71. S. Baert, A.-S. De Pauw, N. Deschacht, Do employer preferences contribute to sticky floors? ILR Rev. 69, 714–736 (2016).
note: Every other entry in both printings of this list numbers itself with a digit and a period, and the article's own printing of this same reference has one. It is the only one of the 128 that is, which is what makes it a slip rather than a convention.

title: The two Ahmed studies are named "Ahmed at al." in all eight places the supplement names them
note: The supplementary materials set "et al." 111 times and "at al." eight, and all eight name one of these two studies: fig. S1.1's two rows, table S2.1's two rows, the captions of figs. S4.5 and S4.6, and fig. S5.62's two rows. It is one string printed eight times rather than eight slips. The deposited data carry the study label in a column of their own, Ahmed at al. (14): Sweden and Ahmed at al. (66): Sweden, and no line of the maintained rewrite spells either of them, so every printing of the misspelling in the supplement is a printing of that one value. The authors' own working figures carry it as well: field_ates_plot.pdf, gender_gradients_plot.pdf and study_manifest.tex in the archived project set it exactly as the published pages do. References 14 and 66, the two studies these labels cite, are set correctly in both printings of the reference list, so nothing here leaves a reader in doubt about which studies are meant.

title: Figure S4.32 misspells an occupation label
note: The row belongs to Dahl and Krog (84): Denmark, and the label is the occupation as the deposited data spell it: dahl_1_occupation_cates.pdf in the authors' archived project prints the same string. The supplement spells "industrial" correctly where it sets it itself, in "industrial relations officials" and "industrial engineering". This is the same study whose occupation count entry 2 corrects, and the two findings are independent: the count is a number the article contradicts elsewhere in its own pages, and the label is a spelling the data carry.

title: Figure S4.28 prints a negative zero
note: The estimate is zero and the minus sign is arithmetic residue. The maintained rewrite returns −1.57e-14 for this row, and 1.43e-14 for the lower secondary teachers (language) row three rows above it, which the same panel prints as 0.00 with no sign. Both differences in means are exactly zero, and what separates the two printings is which side of zero the floating-point remainder fell on. The sign therefore carries no information about the estimate, and it is the only one of the supplement's five rounded zeros that prints a sign. The authors' own carlsson_1_occupation_cates.pdf sets it the same way, so this is the deposit's arithmetic reaching the page rather than the press's typesetting.

title: Reference 123 misabbreviates Social Indicators Research
location: published references, p. 11, and app. references, p. 58
note: The journal is Social Indicators Research, abbreviated Soc. Indic. Res., and the entry attaches a stray s to the abbreviation of Indicators. Crossref, doi 10.1007/s11205-013-0329-4: Lieselotte Blommaert, Marcel Coenders and Frank van Tubergen, "Ethnic Discrimination in Recruitment and Decision Makers' Features", Social Indicators Research 116, 731-754 (2014), whose short container title there is Soc Indic Res. Unlike entries 10 and 11, this one is set IDENTICALLY in both printings of the list, so the second printing reaches it and finds the document agreeing with itself: what it is wrong against is the journal's name rather than the volume's other printing. That is what makes it a note here rather than a twelfth correction, since correcting it would put this edition's two reference lists at odds with the two the paper published.
